2310053.title: Union Environment Minister visits Great Indian Bustard Habitat in Kachchh, Gujarat; Inaugurates GIB Soft Release Centre, Sayara Van Kavach and reviews Mangrove Plantation Efforts
2310053.ministry: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
2310053.body_html:
Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
Union Environment Minister visits Great Indian Bustard Habitat in Kachchh, Gujarat; Inaugurates GIB Soft Release Centre, Sayara Van Kavach and reviews Mangrove Plantation Efforts
Shri Bhupender Yadav flags off Patrolling Vehicles at Naliya; Undertakes Plantation at Sayara and Jakhau and interacts with MISHTI Beneficiaries
Posted On: 14 SEP 2026 3:31PM by PIB Delhi

Kachchh/New Delhi, 14th September, 2026

Union Minister for Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Shri Bhupender Yadav, today visited the Great Indian Bustard (GIB) habitat at Naliya in Kachchh district of Gujarat. He reviewed the ongoing efforts for providing maximum protection to the GIB, with special focus on comprehensive conservation and habitat-management measures being undertaken across the GIB landscape of Kachchh.

The Minister was accompanied by Shri Arjun Modhwadia, Cabinet Minister for Forest and Environment, Climate Change and Science & Technology (Gujarat). Senior officials of the MoEFCC, the Gujarat Forest Department, Wildlife Institute of India (WII) and the Border Security Force (BSF), along with local community members and beneficiaries of afforestation, plantation and coastal livelihood initiatives across Kachchh were also present.

Visited the Great Indian Bustard Habitat in Naliya, Kutch today. Reviewed the ongoing efforts for providing maximum protection to the Great Indian Bustard (GIB) with special focus on comprehensive conservation and habitat-management measures in the GIB landscape of Kutch. Apart from playing an indispensable role in maintaining a healthy ecosystem, GIB serves as a unique cultural symbol of India's arid heritage. To ensure GIB is protected, India is laying great emphasis on its conservation. Towards that end, today inaugurated the Soft Release Centre for GIB in the facility. The Soft Release Centre is equipped with infrastructure designed to support the conservation, monitoring and gradual adaptation of GIBs to the natural environment.

— Bhupender Yadav (@byadavbjp) September 14, 2026

As part of the visit, Shri Yadav inaugurated the Soft Release Centre for the Great Indian Bustard at the facility, and interacted with officials of the Wildlife Institute of India, the Gujarat Forest Department and other stakeholders engaged in the species' conservation. He subsequently held a detailed interaction with public representatives at a 'Khatala Sabha', seeking their continued support in taking the species' conservation initiatives forward.

The Minister was briefed on the significant on-ground progress achieved in the GIB landscape. It included restoration of around 11 sq. km. of grassland infested with the invasive Prosopis juliflora; Raising of 30 km. of predator-proof fencing covering 15 sq. km.; The pioneering 'jump-start' intervention in which infertile eggs laid by wild GIB females were replaced with viable eggs from the conservation breeding programme. Shri Yadav was informed that the resulting chick from the second such attempt has survived beyond the critical first three months in the wild – a landmark result for the species' recovery in Gujarat.

During my visit to the Great Indian Bustard Habitat in Naliya, Kutch, interacted with representatives of the Jat Sumra and Darbar communities in 'Khatala Sabha' to garner their support in the conservation efforts of the Great Indian Bustard. Under the leadership of PM Shri @narendramodi ji, India has been laying emphasis on community-led stewardship for environmental protection and species conservation. The local pastoralist and agricultural groups in Kutch are key to ensuring the success of GIB conservation. Later, flagged off 33 new patrolling and rescue vehicles for forest and wildlife conservation efforts which will be used in various divisions under the Kutch Forest Circle for forest protection, forest development, wildlife protection, field patrolling, monitoring, and quick response activities.

— Bhupender Yadav (@byadavbjp) September 14, 2026

Shri Yadav appreciated the coordinated efforts of the Gujarat Forest Department and the Wildlife Institute of India in advancing this achievement. He also flagged off 33 new patrolling and rescue vehicles for forest and wildlife conservation efforts. These vehicles would be utilised across various divisions under the Kachchh Forest Circle for forest protection, forest development, wildlife protection, field patrolling, monitoring and quick-response activities.

The Minister subsequently visited the Hariyalu Gram plantation in Sayara and was briefed on the Sayara Van Kavach initiative and an associated bee-keeping unit. He undertook tree plantation at the site, inaugurated the Sayara Van Kavach, and witnessed the exchange of a Memorandum of Understanding with the Deendayal Port Authority for plantation activities. The Minister also released the Van Kavach Photobook and interacted with local residents, distributing plant saplings among them.

Inaugurated the Van Kavach at Modpir Dada Temple in Sanyara, Kutch today and planted a bargad sapling along with Shri @arjunmodhwadia and other public representatives. I commend Gujarat for adopting the 'Van Kavach' model to develop dense, green, and biodiversity-rich forest areas within limited spaces in both urban and rural areas. ‘Van Kavach' is not merely tree plantation; it is a natural green protective shield developed around human settlements. It brings together tree plantation, biodiversity conservation, carbon sequestration, environmental education, and public participation.

— Bhupender Yadav (@byadavbjp) September 14, 2026

The Sayara Van Kavach, developed over 9.46 sq. km. site following the Miyawaki method of dense, multi-layered afforestation, comprises over 10,000 saplings across 47 native species suited to the saline, low-water conditions of Kachchh. Shri Yadav was informed that the model is expected to lower local temperatures by 1.5–2°C, aid groundwater recharge, prevent soil erosion, and provide a natural habitat for birds, insects and small wildlife, besides serving as a site for eco-tourism, environmental education and local employment.

At Jakhau, the Minister visited the Mangrove Nursery and undertook mangrove plantation alongside about 50 personnel of the Border Security Force and over 50 local residents at an adjoining site. He viewed a photo exhibition on mangrove plantation efforts in the Kori Creek and Sir Creek areas, visited the seaweed seed bank and interacted with experts, and met seaweed cultivators and beneficiaries of the MISHTI (Mangrove Initiative for Shoreline Habitats & Tangible Incomes) programme.

Planted Avicennia marina, a species of Mangrove, in the Jakhau Mangrove Nursery in Kutch, Gujarat. Under the MISHTI (Mangrove Initiative for Shoreline Habitats & Tangible Incomes) programme initiated by PM Shri @narendramodi ji, Kutch is undertaking large-scale mangrove restoration, scientific nursery development and livelihood initiatives. Against a cumulative plantation target of 29,250 hectares for 2023–24 to 2026–27, mangrove plantation has been completed over 27,652 hectares, including 12,450 hectares in the Kori Creek area. Approximately 3.49 lakh mangrove seedlings have been raised at the Jakhau Mangrove Nursery. Interacted with subject experts to understand the challenges and technological and nature-based solutions to address the same. Kutch is developing a comprehensive model of mangrove conservation by combining large-scale plantation, nurseries, biodiversity conservation, innovative tidal technology, renewable energy, community participation and sustainable livelihoods. Jakhau Mangrove Nursery is a significant example of technology-driven and community-oriented mangrove restoration in Gujarat.

— Bhupender Yadav (@byadavbjp) September 14, 2026

2310033.title: From Coconut Husk to Enterprise: How Coir is transforming Rural lives
2310033.body_html:
Ministry of Micro,Small & Medium Enterprises
From Coconut Husk to Enterprise: How Coir is transforming Rural lives
Coir Emerges as a Catalyst for Rural Entrepreneurship, Women's Empowerment and Sustainable Livelihoods
Posted On: 14 SEP 2026 2:07PM by PIB Delhi

What begins as coconut husk is becoming a source of enterprise and livelihood across India’s coconut-growing regions. Coir, a natural, durable and eco-friendly fibre, has been part of India’s rural economy for generations. Today, entrepreneurs are increasingly converting it into value-added products ranging from mats and ropes to handicrafts, bio-fertilisers and innovative packaging solutions. Behind this transformation are thousands of rural entrepreneurs and artisans who are turning a traditional activity into modern livelihoods. With support from the Ministry of Micro, Small & Medium Enterprises (MSME), particularly through the Coir Board and the Prime Minister’s Employment Generation Programme (PMEGP), coir is becoming a pathway to self-employment, women’s empowerment and local economic growth.

Turning Coir Waste into a Thriving Enterprise:

  1. One Enterprise, 120 Women, Countless Opportunities

In Kadiyam, East Godavari district of Andhra Pradesh, Ms. Allam Gowthamy transformed coconut fibre and coir waste into a successful enterprise. She received specialised training at the Coir Board Training Centre, Dhawaleswaram and established Adigo Coir Products in 2024–25 with a project cost of ₹10 lakh, supported by a ₹6.50 lakh bank loan and PMEGP assistance. The unit now produces eco-friendly doormats, ropes, decorative dolls and handicrafts.


  

The enterprise has achieved an annual turnover of around ₹35 lakh and a profit of approximately ₹10 lakh, while generating direct employment for six women. But her impact extends beyond her own enterprise. She has trained nearly 120 women in coir mat weaving, rope making and handicraft production, helping them develop livelihood opportunities. Her success has also inspired around 5 additional coir units in nearby areas with Prime Minister’s Employment Generation Programme.

2. Shri Surendran’s Green Coir Success Story

Turning coir pith into an opportunity for sustainable agriculture, Shri P. Surendran established Sampoorna Plus Agro Fertilizer Enterprises (SAFE) in Kozhikode, Kerala, in November 2024. With training and technical support from the Coir Board, Kannur and Central Coir Research Institute (CCRI), Kalavoor, he began producing eco-friendly coir pith bio-fertilizer that improves soil fertility and moisture retention.

 

In just one year his enterprise has built a customer base of 500+, sold over 20 tonnes of bio-fertilizer and generated a turnover of ₹13 lakh, with a profit of ₹4 lakh in FY 2024–25. The unit also employs five workers, including two women, creating local livelihood opportunities. From coir waste to a sustainable business, his journey shows how innovation and technical support can create new business opportunities from materials that might otherwise have limited economic value.

Why Coir Matters to Rural India

Coir is one of India’s oldest natural fibres. Organised coir production in India began in 1859 with the establishment of the first coir factory in Alappuzha, Kerala. Since then, the sector has grown across major coconut-producing regions. India is the world’s largest producer of coir and accounts for more than 80 per cent of global coir fibre production. The industry is also closely linked with women’s livelihoods. Women account for nearly 80 per cent of those engaged in fibre extraction and spinning. This makes coir an important rural livelihood sector—connecting coconut farmers, workers, women artisans, cooperatives, entrepreneurs, manufacturers and exporters.

From Fibre to Finished Product

The potential of coir extends well beyond the production of raw fibre. Through processing, design and innovation, coir can be transformed into a wide range of higher-value products, including:

  • Mats and doormats
  • Ropes and yarn
  • Brushes and other household products
  • Decorative items and handicrafts
  • Garden and horticulture products
  • Innovative and eco-friendly packaging solutions

Supporting the Coir Value Chain

The Coir Board, a statutory body under the Ministry of MSME, works to strengthen the sector through skill development, technology, research, market promotion, exports and welfare initiatives.

The Coir Vikas Yojana (CVY) supports areas such as technology and research, skill development, women’s training, domestic and international market promotion, industry development and worker welfare. The objective is to enable people associated with the coir sector to acquire new skills, adopt better technology, produce quality products and access larger markets. At the same time, exhibitions, fairs, showrooms and export promotion activities are helping coir producers showcase their products and connect with new customers and markets.

Innovation: Giving Coir a New Identity

The Central Coir Research Institute has developed eco-friendly coir rail wheel axle packaging cups as an alternative to HDPE plastic cups. Such innovations show how a traditional natural fibre can find applications in modern industries while supporting environmentally responsible production.

A Fibre with a Bigger Purpose

The stories of Shri Allam Gowthamy and Shri G. Sabu illustrate the changing face of India’s coir sector. With skills, finance, technology, research and market support, India’s traditional coir sector is steadily moving towards higher-value products and modern enterprises—turning locally available resources into opportunities for entrepreneurship and prosperity.

For more information, visit at: https://coirboard.gov.in/

***

2310017.title: Export of Power to Nepal Approved
2310017.body_html:
Ministry of Power
Export of Power to Nepal Approved
Posted On: 14 SEP 2026 1:38PM by PIB Delhi

Ministry of Power has accorded approval for the export of power, for 18 hours a day (00:00 hours to 18:00 hours) to Nepal Electricity Authority from 13 September 2026 to 31 December, 2026.

Approval has been given for upto 600MW of export through Muzaffarpur - Dhalkebar 400 kV D/c line and upto 54 MW through Tanakpur - Mahendranagar 132 kV S/c line. The quantum of power to be exported from January 2027, will be reviewed in December,2026.

The recent floods have caused significant damage to hydropower infrastructure in Nepal, reducing its domestic power generation capacity and creating an additional requirement for electricity. The approval will help Nepal meet its power requirements during this difficult period and further strengthen the close and longstanding energy cooperation between India and Nepal.

India remains committed to supporting Nepal and strengthening bilateral cooperation in the energy sector.

2310000.title: INS MYSORE CONCLUDES PARTICIPATION IN THE 4TH EDITION OF EXERCISE SAMUDRA LAKSAMANA AT LUMUT, MALAYSIA
2310000.body_html:
Ministry of Defence
INS MYSORE CONCLUDES PARTICIPATION IN THE 4TH EDITION OF EXERCISE SAMUDRA LAKSAMANA AT LUMUT, MALAYSIA
Posted On: 14 SEP 2026 1:14PM by PIB Delhi

As part of the Indian Navy’s Operational Deployment, Indian Naval Ship Mysore participated in the 4th edition of Exercise Samudra Laksamana with the Royal Malaysian Navy at Lumut, Malaysia, from 09 to 12 Sep 2026.

The exercise provided an opportunity for the Indian Navy and the Royal Malaysian Navy to engage across a broad spectrum of professional and operational activities. The harbour phase featured professional exchanges and interactions between personnel of the two Navies, facilitating the sharing of experiences and fostering greater mutual understanding.

The engagement progressed to the operational phase at sea, during which INS Mysore exercised with Royal Malaysian Navy ships KD Lekir and KD Gagah Samudera. The participating ships undertook coordinated maritime evolutions, providing an opportunity to enhance interoperability, refine operational coordination and strengthen their ability to operate together effectively.

The completion of the exercise reflects the growing depth and maturity of naval cooperation between India and Malaysia. It also highlights the value of sustained professional engagement and practical cooperation in building greater operational understanding between the two maritime forces.

Exercise ‘Samudra Laksamana’ marks another significant engagement in the expanding India–Malaysia maritime partnership. Building upon the momentum generated by recent bilateral engagements, including the 12th India–Malaysia Sub Committee Meeting held on 01 Jul 2026, the exercise has further consolidated the foundations of cooperation between the two Navies.

2309999.title: Shri Manohar Lal celebrates Hindi Diwas with Indian community in Houston
2309999.body_html:
Ministry of Power
Shri Manohar Lal celebrates Hindi Diwas with Indian community in Houston
Visits NASA’s Johnson Space Center; engages with Indian diaspora ahead of G20 Energy Abundance Ministerial Meeting
Posted On: 14 SEP 2026 1:07PM by PIB Delhi

Shri Manohar Lal, Union Minister for Power and Housing & Urban Affairs, who is in Houston, USA, to participate in the G20 Energy Abundance Ministerial Meeting, undertook a series of engagements on September 13, 2026, reflecting India’s cultural connect with the diaspora, commitment to environmental responsibility and expanding India–US cooperation in emerging areas.

Shri Manohar Lal attended (13.09.2026) the event to mark Hindi Diwas 2026 organised by the Consulate General of India, Houston, in collaboration with the International Hindi Association – Houston Chapter. The gathering celebrated the richness, inclusivity and vibrancy of Hindi and brought together Hindi enthusiasts from across the region. Shri Manohar Lal addressed the gathering and appreciated the efforts towards promoting Hindi and strengthening cultural ties between India and the Indian diaspora.

During his visit to the Consulate General of India, Shri Manohar Lal planted a tree under the ‘Ek Ped Maa Ke Naam’ initiative. The plantation also marked the beginning of Swachhata Hi Seva 2026 at the Consulate, as part of the national campaign being observed with the theme “Swachhata Mein Sahbhag, Swachh Bharat, Viksit Bharat”, reinforcing the values of public participation and environmental responsibility.

During the day (13.09.2026), Shri Manohar Lal also visited NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston. He undertook a tour of the facility and held discussions on opportunities to further strengthen India–US collaboration in the space sector. Shri Manohar Lal thanked Mr. William T. Harris, President and CEO, Space Center Houston, for the warm welcome and for personally guiding him during the visit.

In the evening (13.09.2026), Shri Manohar Lal attended a public reception organised by the Indian diaspora at India House, Houston. A diverse cross-section of the community, including professionals, entrepreneurs, students, cultural leaders and representatives of regional associations, participated in the reception. Consul General Shri D.C. Manjunath welcomed Shri Manohar Lal and expressed appreciation for his interaction with the Indian diaspora during his visit for the G20 Energy Abundance Ministerial Meeting.

Meanwhile, the Haryanvi community, represented by HARIT, also interacted with Shri Manohar Lal. The Minister lauded the strong and enduring people-to-people ties between India and the United States and the valuable contribution of the Indian diaspora to the economic, cultural and social fabric of the country.

The engagements on September 13, 2026 reflected the multifaceted dimensions of India–US relations, encompassing G20 cooperation, cultural and people-to-people ties, environmental responsibility and collaboration in advanced technology and space.

Over the next three days (14-16 September 2026), the Minister will participate in the G20 Energy Abundance Ministerial Meeting which brings together Ministers and senior representatives of G20 members to deliberate on key issues relating to energy security, affordability, accessibility and the evolving global energy landscape. India’s participation underscores its commitment to constructive international cooperation and advancing solutions for secure, reliable, affordable and sustainable energy.

2309991.title: Message of Union Home Minister and Minister of Cooperation Shri Amit Shah on Hindi Diwas 2026
2309991.body_html:
Ministry of Home Affairs
Message of Union Home Minister and Minister of Cooperation Shri Amit Shah on Hindi Diwas 2026
Posted On: 14 SEP 2026 12:54PM by PIB Delhi

Dear fellow citizens,

Warm greetings to all of you on the occasion of Hindi Diwas!

Our country is a unique land of linguistic diversity and rich cultural heritage. Many people say that the fact that we have different languages is a weakness, but I believe that having so many languages is our greatest strength. Every language carries with it a history, folk traditions and a distinct worldview, which also help carry forward the values and cultural ethos of our younger generations. This linguistic plurality strengthens the spirit of ‘Unity in Diversity’ that defines India. Language is not merely a means of communication; it is the memory of a society and its sense of self.

Amid this diversity, Hindi has played an important role as a language of dialogue, communication and coordination, bringing together people from different sections and communities across the country. The development of Hindi can truly be meaningful only when it progresses alongside the respect, preservation and promotion of all Indian languages. Hindi is not a competitor to any language; rather, it is an important link for fostering a sense of affinity and dialogue among Indian languages and strengthening national unity. The most beautiful testimony to this truth lies in our own history. Swami Dayanand Saraswati Ji was a native Gujarati speaker, yet he wrote Satyarth Prakash in Hindi. Mahatma Gandhi established the Dakshina Bharat Hindi Prachar Sabha in Madras in 1918. Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose was a Bengali speaker, yet he adopted Hindi as the language of communication of the Azad Hind Fauj and gave the nation the inspiring slogan ‘Jai Hind’. Thus, people from diverse linguistic backgrounds have made the greatest contribution towards making Hindi a language of communication among the people. The immense contribution of these great personalities, whose mother tongue was never Hindi, remains a source of inspiration for all of us.

My own mother tongue is also Gujarati, but whenever I travel to any part of the country, the language that directly connects me with the common people there is Hindi. If we look at the journey of Hindi, we can see reflected in it the journey of the entire nation. From the Padavali of Vidyapati in the Adikal period and the heroic ballads of Prithviraj Raso, to the remarkable era of the Bhakti period—when Tulsidas Ji took the story of Lord Rama to every household and Surdas Ji gave a voice to the tender expression of parental affection.

During the freedom movement, the ideals of Swaraj, Swadeshi and Swabhasha infused new energy into the national consciousness. Our freedom fighters, too, had realised that the vision of Swaraj would remain incomplete without pride in our own language and identity. After Independence, Indian languages became the means of nation-building, governance and taking the development to every citizen. Hindi, along with all other Indian languages, played an important role in spreading the message of social awakening, national unity and the idea of freedom to every section of society. Carrying forward this rich legacy, the Constituent Assembly adopted Hindi as the Official Language of the Union of India on 14 September 1949. However, a paradox also emerged after Independence. While we attained political freedom, the values of our own language, our own culture and our self-respect were pushed to the margins.

Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi Ji, from the Red Fort, called upon the nation to free itself from this mindset of colonialism, and language has a pivotal role to play in this. The transformation of Rajpath into Kartavya Path was not merely a change of name. Replacing the colonial, punishment-oriented laws enacted by the British with three people-centric laws—the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita and the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam—was not merely a change in terminology. It represents the restoration of our national self-pride.

Today, the National Education Policy places the mother tongue at the centre of education. Engineering and medical education is being imparted in Indian languages, and competitive examinations are being conducted in multiple Indian languages.

On the occasion of the 80th Independence Day, the Prime Minister, from the Red Fort, called for ‘Saptadhara of Shakti’—the seven streams of strength—for building a Viksit Bharat. The seventh stream is India’s soft power. The greatest carrier of any nation’s soft power is its language. Yoga, Ayurveda, literature, cinema and our cultural strength—all reach the world through our languages.

There was once a concern that in the age of technology, Indian languages might be left behind. However, under the Modi Government, Hindi, along with all other Indian languages, is witnessing a golden era of technological advancement.

The ‘Bharati’ tool, an Artificial Intelligence-based tool developed by the Department of Official Language, is making communication among Indian languages more seamless today. The ‘Hindi Shabd Sindhu’, a digital dictionary with more than 8.27 lakh entries, has emerged as a rich platform for knowledge sharing. The ‘Indian Language Section’, established in 2024, is facilitating administrative communication in Indian languages. AI and translation technologies have brought down the barriers of language. Today, every Indian can think in their own language and communicate with the entire world. At the same time, during the tenure of the Modi Government, the Parliamentary Committee on Official Language has submitted four new volumes of its reports to the Hon’ble President.

At the end, I would like to say something to the youth. Learn as many languages of the world as you can, but never abandon your own language. I would also urge all parents across the country to make it a point to communicate with your children in their mother tongue. There can be no greater inferiority complex than the thought, “If I speak in my own language, I will be considered inferior.”

Language is what connects us with our mother, our soil, our history and our culture. This year also marks the 150th anniversary of the composition of the national song, ‘Vande Mataram’—a song that transformed language into a weapon of freedom.

Let us, on this occasion, resolve to make Hindi and all Indian languages powerful instruments in our journey towards building a Viksit Bharat by 2047.

Once again, my heartfelt greetings to all of you on Official Language Day. Vande Mataram!

***

2309984.title: Prime Minister Narendra Modi to Inaugurate Fifth Edition of SEMICON India 2026 on September 17
2309984.body_html:
Ministry of Electronics & IT
Prime Minister Narendra Modi to Inaugurate Fifth Edition of SEMICON India 2026 on September 17
India’s Biggest Semiconductor and Electronics Event to be held at Yashobhoomi, New Delhi, from September 17–19
SEMICON India 2026 to Bring Together Over 600 Exhibitors, 300 International Companies and Delegations from More Than 40 Countries
‘Silicon to Systems: Building the Ecosystem’ to Showcase India’s Growing Capabilities Across the Semiconductor Value Chain
Posted On: 14 SEP 2026 12:44PM by PIB Delhi

The fifth edition of SEMICON India 2026, India’s premier semiconductor and electronics conference and exhibition, will be held from September 17–19, 2026 at Yashobhoomi (India International Convention & Expo Centre), New Delhi. Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi will inaugurate the event on September 17, 2026, marking the beginning of three days of high-level deliberations, industry engagement and showcasing of India’s rapidly expanding semiconductor and electronics ecosystem.

Organised jointly by the India Semiconductor Mission (ISM), Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), Government of India, and SEMI, the global industry association representing the semiconductor and electronics design and manufacturing ecosystem, SEMICON India 2026 will bring together global semiconductor and electronics companies, industry leaders, policymakers, investors, researchers, academia, start-ups and students on a common platform to exchange ideas, forge partnerships and shape the future of India’s semiconductor and electronics ecosystem.

With the theme “Silicon to Systems: Building the Ecosystem,” SEMICON India 2026 marks an important milestone in India’s semiconductor journey. It comes at a time when strong policy momentum, growing industry execution and rising global demand for trusted and resilient semiconductor supply chains are converging to position India as an increasingly important player across the global semiconductor value chain.

This is what makes SEMICON India 2026 much more than an exhibition. Over three days at Yashobhoomi, more than 600 exhibitors, including 300 international companies, will come together across 15,000 square metres of space, alongside 150+ renowned speakers sharing their knowledge, experience and insights. Six country pavilions and 12 state pavilions will sit alongside a startup showcase, a student hackathon, a workforce development pavilion and a Women’s Forum, each offering a window into a different part of the semiconductor ecosystem that India has been steadily building over the past five years.

Showcasing India’s Semiconductor Ecosystem

SEMICON India 2026 will adopt a comprehensive value-chain approach, showcasing the journey from semiconductor materials and manufacturing to advanced packaging, design,

electronics and systems. The new ‘Sand to Silicon to Systems’ Value Chain Experience will

provide visitors with an integrated view of the semiconductor ecosystem and demonstrate India's expanding capabilities across different stages of the value chain.

The exhibition will feature six country pavilions and twelve State Government pavilions, along with a dedicated Startup Pavilion, Innovation Showcase, Startup Pitch Competition, Student Hackathon and Workforce Development Pavilion. The Startup Pavilion will showcase around 40 startups, while the Workforce Development Pavilion will provide a dedicated platform for talent, skills and career opportunities in the microelectronics sector.

The event will provide an important opportunity for Indian and international companies to explore partnerships, investment opportunities, technology collaborations and supply-chain linkages, further strengthening India's position as a trusted global semiconductor partner.

Comprehensive Conference Programme

The three-day conference programme will feature high-level keynotes, panel discussions and strategic sessions focusing on emerging trends and critical areas across the semiconductor and electronics ecosystem, including semiconductor manufacturing and technology, artificial

intelligence, supply-chain resilience, advanced packaging, materials and equipment, chip design, research and development, startups, innovation and talent development.

The programme will also include six International Country Roundtables, a dedicated session on Women Empowerment & Leadership, a Workforce Development Session, and a special session titled “Stronger Together: Industry Associations Collaborating for India’s ESDM Growth.”

The event is expected to feature participation from leading global and Indian companies across the semiconductor and electronics ecosystem, including ASML, Applied Materials, Teradyne, Infineon, Ebara, Jabil, IBM Research, NXP, Tata Electronics, Micron, Merck KGaA, Rapidus, Lam Research, CG Power, Uno Minda, Advantest, Tokyo Electron and several other major industry players.

From Policy to Production

SEMICON India 2026 is being held at a significant juncture in India's semiconductor journey.

Under the Semicon India Programme, the Government has approved 12 semiconductor

projects aimed at establishing a robust and resilient semiconductor ecosystem in the country.

The progress has now moved beyond project approvals, with three of the 12 projects approved under Semicon 1.0 having commenced commercial production. At the same time, the Union Cabinet has approved the next phase, Semicon 2.0, with six major pillars aimed at further accelerating the development of India's semiconductor ecosystem.

The Government is also supporting semiconductor research, innovation and design.

State-of-the-art electronic design automation tools have been made available to more than 400 academic institutions and 105 startups, while 24 startups have been approved under the Design Linked Incentive (DLI) Scheme to design innovative semiconductor products and applications.

These initiatives are aimed at developing capabilities across the semiconductor value chain and creating a strong foundation for India's transition towards a globally competitive semiconductor and electronics manufacturing ecosystem.

India as a Trusted Global Semiconductor Partner

The global semiconductor industry is undergoing rapid transformation, driven by the expansion of artificial intelligence, digital technologies, advanced computing, electric mobility,

telecommunications and other emerging technologies. At the same time, the need for diversified, resilient and trusted semiconductor supply chains has assumed greater importance.

Against this backdrop, India is emerging as a significant destination for semiconductor design, manufacturing, research, innovation and investment, supported by progressive government policies, a large pool of skilled professionals, strong domestic demand and growing interest from global industry.

The global semiconductor market, valued at around USD 796 billion in 2025, is projected to surpass USD 2 trillion by 2030. India’s semiconductor demand, currently estimated at around USD 50 billion, is projected to reach around USD 103 billion by 2030, highlighting the country’s significant growth potential in the semiconductor sector.

The theme “Silicon to Systems: Building the Ecosystem” captures India’s transition from building credibility to demonstrating capability across the semiconductor value chain. The event aims to accelerate collaboration, investment, innovation and ecosystem integration, while strengthening India’s position as a trusted global partner in the semiconductor industry.

SEMICON India has evolved into an important annual convergence point for global industry leaders, policymakers, researchers, start-ups and investors. The 2026 edition seeks to build on this momentum by providing a platform for collaboration, technology partnerships, investment, talent development and knowledge exchange, further strengthening the ecosystem and supporting India’s vision of emerging as a global hub for semiconductor and electronics manufacturing.

Visitor Registration Now Open for SEMICON India 2026 Register now at: https://portal.semiconindia.org/register

About SEMICON India

SEMICON India is India's premier semiconductor conference and exhibition, jointly organised by the India Semiconductor Mission (ISM), Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), Government of India, and SEMI. It serves as a flagship platform for bringing together the global semiconductor and electronics ecosystem to advance collaboration, innovation, manufacturing, investment and talent development, while supporting India's vision of becoming a trusted global hub for semiconductor and electronics manufacturing.

About India Semiconductor Mission

The India Semiconductor Mission (ISM) aims to build a strong semiconductor and display ecosystem and position India as a global hub for electronics manufacturing and design. ISM

serves as the nodal agency for the efficient and seamless implementation of semiconductor and display schemes and works in consultation with Government ministries, departments, agencies, industry and academia.

2309982.title: DRI seizes more than 362 MT Pakistan-origin dry dates under ‘Operation Deep Manifest’
2309982.body_html:
Ministry of Finance
DRI seizes more than 362 MT Pakistan-origin dry dates under ‘Operation Deep Manifest’ 
Posted On: 14 SEP 2026 12:23PM by PIB Delhi

In a significant crackdown on attempts to circumvent India’s prohibition on imports from Pakistan, the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence (DRI), has seized more than 362 metric tonnes of Pakistan-origin dry dates.

Acting on specific intelligence, DRI officers intercepted 13 containers of dry dates imported by a Mumbai-based firm at CFS Ambad, Nashik. The consignments had arrived from Jebel Ali, UAE, with import documents declaring the UAE as the country of origin.

Preliminary investigation revealed a carefully orchestrated transshipment arrangement designed to conceal the Pakistan-origin of the goods. The dry dates were initially shipped from Karachi Port, Pakistan, to Jebel Ali Port, UAE, in one set of containers aboard one vessel. At Jebel Ali, the goods were merely transshipped and trans

ferred to another set of containers and loaded onto a different vessel for onward shipment to India through entities operated by Pakistani nationals.

Following the Pahalgam terror attack, the Government of India, in the interest of national security, imposed a complete prohibition on the direct or indirect import or transit of all goods originating in or exported from Pakistan, with effect from 2 May 2025, vide DGFT Notification No. 06/2025-26 dated 2 May 2025. In response, DRI, under “Operation Deep Manifest”, has been consistently identifying, intercepting and seizing Pakistan-origin goods attempted to be imported into India through third-country routing.

The seizure underscores DRI’s sustained resolve to identify, disrupt and dismantle sophisticated networks seeking to circumvent trade prohibitions through misdeclaration, transshipment and manipulation of documentation, thereby safeguarding national security and straightening supply chain integrity.

  1. All India Wholesale Price Index (WPI) inflation for August 2026 is 9.92 per cent on year-on-year (YoY) basis, compared to 9.78 per cent in July 2026. The index for All Commodities for August 2026 stands at 110.8, whereas it was 110.0 in July 2026.
  2. YoY inflation rates for major groups, namely, Primary Articles, Fuel and Power, and Manufactured Products are 7.76 per cent, 22.93 per cent, and 8.37 per cent, respectively in August 2026, compared to 8.52 per cent, 20.05 per cent, and 8.29 per cent, respectively in July 2026. The indices for Primary Articles, Fuel and Power, and Manufactured Products are 118.1, 108.3 and 108.8, respectively, in August 2026, whereas they were 117.2, 105.4, and 108.4, respectively, in July 2026.

2309962.title: Commercial Coal Mine Auctions: Powering Aatmanirbhar Bharat Through Transparency
2309962.body_html:
Ministry of Coal
Commercial Coal Mine Auctions: Powering Aatmanirbhar Bharat Through Transparency
Posted On: 14 SEP 2026 11:19AM by PIB Delhi

Coal block allocation in India has undergone a significant transformation over the past decade. Following the Supreme Court's cancellation of 204 coal blocks in 2014, allocation moved to a transparent, rules-based process. The launch of commercial coal mine auctions by the Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi on 18 June 2020 marked the next major step. Six years on, it has become one of the most consequential structural reforms in the mining sector, delivering benefits shared transparently across industry, the exchequer and coal-bearing communities.

The entire process has been kept transparent. Bidding is conducted online in two stages on the MSTC platform, with bid documents decrypted and opened live in front of bidders. There is no end-use restriction, 100% FDI is allowed through the automatic route, and upfront payments are kept low and adjustable against future revenue share, keeping the field open to smaller and newer players. The Policy has been such a success that 147 coal mines have been auctioned till date with 44 new companies winning a coal mine. The Policy has not only attracted private players but also legacy coal PSUs like Coal India's own subsidiaries — Western Coalfields Limited (WCL) and Northern Coalfields Limited (NCL), traditionally only producers and sellers of coal — have themselves stepped in as bidders for blocks in recent rounds, competing on exactly the same terms as private players.

Every auctioned block contributes a strong share to the states in the form of revenue share (the competitively bid revenue share, additional to royalty), Royalty (statutory, to the state), DMF contributions (ploughed back into the mining district via PMKKKY), NMET contributions (funding future exploration) and GST. Since 2020, 147 coal blocks have been auctioned across nine states, projected to generate approx.₹47,500 crore in annual revenue, ₹55,000 crore in capital investment and 4.9 lakh jobs. In the Financial Year 2025-26, the total revenue generated (from upfront & premium payment) from allocated commercial mines was about Rs. 3090 Cr.

The revenue story runs alongside a production story. Coal output from only commercial mines grew from 12.55 million tonnes in FY 2023-24 to 23.51 million tonnes in FY 2024-25. Captive and commercial blocks together produced about 210 MT in FY 2025-26, crossing the 200 million tonne mark for the first time. A decade earlier the figure stood at 28.8 MT, hence showcasing a compound annual growth of about 22 per cent over the period. Every additional tonne mined domestically is a tonne that need not be imported, directly supporting India's push toward self-reliance in coal.

Transparent, technology-enabled bidding that keeps attracting new entrants; a level playing field open enough that even government miners now compete for blocks rather than being handed them; and a revenue-sharing design — royalty, premium, DMF and NMET stacked together — that has nearly tripled states' coal revenue in a decade: together, these make the commercial coal mine auction regime a genuine win-win for states, industry, local communities and the nation's energy security alike.

2309950.title: Data Centres in India Infrastructure for the Digital Age
2309950.body_html:
PIB Backgrounder
Data Centres in India Infrastructure for the Digital Age
Posted On: 14 SEP 2026 11:05AM by PIB Delhi

Data centres are the invisible engines powering India’s digital life. They support banking, e-Governance and online services every second. As emerging technologies drive rapid data growth, the Government is building a supportive policy ecosystem. Infrastructure status, fiscal incentives and clean energy adoption are strengthening India’s data centre ecosystem.

Strengthening India's Digital Infrastructure through Data Centres

India’s digital economy is entering a new phase of rapid growth and technological transformation. Digitalisation is reshaping productivity, competitiveness and service delivery across sectors. As digital services expand, they are generating unprecedented demand for computing capacity, data storage and high-speed connectivity. Meeting this demand requires infrastructure that can operate continuously, securely and at scale. Data centres provide this critical foundation, powering the digital services that increasingly drive India’s economy and governance.

A data centre is a secure facility that houses computing, storage and networking equipment. It stores, processes, manages and distributes large volumes of digital information. These capabilities support online banking, e-Governance, digital payments, cloud computing and other emerging technologies.

Modern data centres integrate computing, networking, power, cooling, security and management systems. These systems work continuously to maintain reliable operations, data security and uninterrupted digital services. As India’s digital economy expands, resilient data centres are becoming a strategic infrastructure for innovation, competitiveness and sustained digital growth.

Inside a Data Centre: The Technologies Powering Digital Services

A data centre relies on a reliable power infrastructure to ensure uninterrupted operation of critical equipment. Data centre computers can never turn off—not even for a millisecond. Uninterruptible Power Supplies (UPS) provide immediate backup during electrical interruptions. Backup generators and electrical distribution systems provide additional resilience during prolonged power disruptions. Continuous operations of this scale requires  cooling systems to maintain suitable operating conditions for the computing equipment. Heating, Ventilation and Air Conditioning (HVAC) systems regulate temperature and airflow within the facility. Advanced airflow management and liquid cooling further improve thermal efficiency and reliability.

The Information Technology (IT) infrastructure then performs the core computing functions. Servers process information and run digital applications. Storage systems securely hold large volumes of data using Hard Disk Drives (HDDs) and Solid-State Drives (SSDs). Security systems protect equipment, networks and data from physical and digital threats.

Networking equipment, including routers and high-speed switches, enables data exchange within and beyond the facility. Fiber-optic connections provide high-speed communication between the data centre and external networks.

Finally, management software monitors the systems and helps optimize the use of computing resources efficiently. Virtualisation allows multiple virtual machines to run on one physical server, improving resource use. Imagine taking one large house and dividing it into several separate apartments. Virtualization allows one physical computer to run multiple virtual "mini-computers" inside it, maximizing resource efficiency. Automation tools manage workloads, support maintenance and help identify operational problems.

From Click to Response: How a Data Centre Handles Your Request

Every digital request begins with a simple action, such as opening an app, checking a bank balance or accessing a document. Behind the instant response, the request travels through a network to a data centre, where multiple systems work together to process it securely and efficiently.

The security layer first checks the request and protects the system from cyber threats. The load balancer then directs the request to an available server, helping distribute the workload efficiently.

The application server processes the request and determines what information or service is required. If necessary, it uses an Application Programming Interface (API) to communicate with other applications or services.

The database server then retrieves the required information and sends it back to the application server. Once processed, the information travels back through the network and reaches the user’s device.

This entire process can take just 1–2 seconds, enabling fast and seamless digital services. This interconnected chain— Connect → Receive → Network → Process → Store → Secure → Respond—allows cloud services, e-governance platforms and Artificial Intelligence (AI) applications to deliver information reliably and at scale. It shows why modern data centres are far more than storage facilities; they are the digital infrastructure that enables everyday online services.

In Simple Terms: The Behind-the-Scenes Team

  • Network = The Corridors & Intercom, the internal hallways that connect the whole team so they can pass information to each other instantly.
  • Security Layer = The Security Guard, inspects your request at the entrance for safety.
  • Load Balancer = The Traffic Cop, directs incoming digital traffic so no single server gets overwhelmed
  • Application Server = The Chef, takes your order, figures out what information or recipe is needed.
  • API = The Waiter, acts as a messenger.
  • Database Server = The Digital Vault, where details are locked away and retrieved when needed.

 

Status of Data Centers in India

India’s data-centre journey has evolved alongside the rapid expansion of e-Governance and digital services. Rising citizen expectations for online services are increasing demand for robust data-centre infrastructure. The National Informatics Centre (NIC) has established state-of-the-art National Data Centres across the country. These include facilities at NIC Headquarters in Delhi, Pune, Hyderabad and Bhubaneswar. NIC has also established 37 smaller Data Centres at various State Capitals. These facilities provide reliable digital services to Government institutions at different levels. They support round-the-clock operations, system management and skilled onsite personnel.

India’s rapidly expanding digital economy is further strengthening demand for secure and reliable data infrastructure. Installed data-centre power capacity stood at around 375 MW in 2020. It has increased to 1.57 GW as of August 2026. The capacity is projected to expand further to nearly 8 GW by 2030. Investments of nearly USD 70 billion are already underway in India’s data centre sector, with an additional USD 90 billion in announced projects, highlighting the scale of expansion and reflecting strong investor confidence.

Enabling Policy Environment for Data Centres

The Government has strengthened the data-centre ecosystem through targeted policy and fiscal measures. In the Union Budget 2022–23, data centres were included in the Harmonized List of Infrastructure. This accorded infrastructure status to data centres and facilitated greater access to credit for digital infrastructure. The measure also supported investment and expansion of India’s data-centre capacity.

Infrastructure Status in Simple Terms

Giving data centres "Infrastructure Status" treats them like national highways, airports, and power grids, granting them access to easier and cheaper long-term loans.

The Union Budget 2026–27 further introduced a tax holiday for eligible foreign cloud service providers until 2047. The incentive applies to global operations using India-based data-centre infrastructure. It covers Tax Years 2026–27 to 2046–47 for notified foreign companies. These measures strengthen India’s investment environment for data centres and cloud infrastructure.

Linked Ecosystem Schemes Supporting Data Centre Growth

  • The second phase of the Semicon India Programme (Semicon 2.0) was approved by the Union Cabinet on 15.07.2026, with an outlay of ₹1,27,500 crore under the India Semiconductor Mission (ISM). It aims to holistically build a trusted and resilient semiconductor ecosystem in the country.
  • The IndiaAI Mission was approved with a total budget outlay of ₹10,371.92 crore to build a comprehensive AI ecosystem in the country. The AI ecosystem being fostered under the Mission is a key driver of data centre growth in India.
  • The Electronics Components Manufacturing Scheme (ECMS) has also received higher financial support. Its allocation increased from ₹22,000 crore to ₹40,000 crore.
  • The Government of India has also launched PLI Scheme 2.0 for IT Hardware to create a robust domestic manufacturing ecosystem for IT hardware (such as servers), attract large investments, reduce import reliance, and make India a trusted global supply chain hub.

Sustaining the Data Centre Sector: Energy and Water Planning

Data centre capacity is expanding rapidly, making energy and resource efficiency increasingly important. Data centres require reliable electricity and efficient cooling systems for continuous operations. According to the Central Electricity Authority (CEA), Ministry of Power, demand could reach 17 GW by 2031–32. As the sector is expanding, the Government is also promoting cleaner energy and efficient resource use to support sustainable sectoral growth.

Renewable Energy & Clean Power

The Government is promoting renewable energy through several key initiatives. These include the Green Energy Open Access Rules, Green Energy Corridor Scheme and National Green Hydrogen Mission. The National Programme on High Efficiency Solar PV Modules and Solar Park Scheme further support clean-energy deployment. These measures improve access to cleaner and more reliable power for energy-intensive digital infrastructure.

SHANTI Act & Clean Power

The Sustainable Harnessing and Advancement of Nuclear Energy for Transforming India (SHANTI) Act strengthens the clean-power ecosystem. It supports reliable nuclear power for emerging sectors, including Artificial Intelligence and data centres. The framework also enables future deployment of Small Modular Reactors and Micro Nuclear Reactors.

BIS Standards for Data Centres

The Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) has developed standards for data-centre efficiency. Its technical committee LITD 31 covers Cloud Computing, Information Technology and Data Centres. BIS has published standards covering Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) and Carbon Usage Effectiveness (CUE). These standards also address Cooling Efficiency Ratio (CER) and Water Usage Effectiveness (WUE).

In Simple Terms

PUE and WUE - serve as green mileage ratings to measure how efficiently a facility uses electricity and water.

CUE measures how much carbon pollution a data centre produces for every bit of electricity its computers use.

CER measures how efficiently the cooling systems (like fans, chilled water pipes, or liquid coolant) remove that heat relative to the electricity they consume.

Energy and Water Efficiency Standards

The Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE) has notified the Energy Conservation Building Code (ECBC) 2017. It also notified the Energy Conservation and Sustainable Building Code (ECSBC) 2024. These codes prescribe energy-efficiency and water-conservation norms for buildings. They also include provisions relevant to data-centre infrastructure.

Advanced Cooling and Water Management

Data-centre water requirements depend on the cooling technologies deployed. Groundwater extraction, including for industrial purposes, is regulated under guidelines issued by the Ministry of Jal Shakti. AI infrastructure is driving adoption of advanced cooling technologies in data centres. These include direct-to-chip liquid cooling, adiabatic cooling and immersion cooling. Closed-loop liquid cooling systems are also emerging as resource-efficient solutions.

Way Forward

India’s data-centre growth reflects a steady policy journey towards a resilient and sovereign digital infrastructure. It is increasingly important for data sovereignty, digital trust, economic competitiveness and technological self-reliance. The expansion of cloud and Artificial Intelligence infrastructure is creating new opportunities for innovation and economic growth. However, this growth also requires responsible governance of data, technology, energy and digital infrastructure. A technology governance approach can help balance innovation with security, sustainability, accountability and public interest. This requires strong standards, robust cybersecurity, responsible data practices and efficient resource management. It also calls for greater domestic capabilities across computing, semiconductors, energy and critical digital infrastructure. As India advances towards Viksit Bharat by 2047, data centres can serve as a foundational layer of the digital economy.

2309882.title: Shri Bhupender Yadav reviews progress of Great Indian Bustard Conservation, Grassland Restoration and Project Cheetah at Bhuj; Releases Gujarat Action Plan for GIB Conservation
2309882.ministry: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
2309882.body_html:
Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
Shri Bhupender Yadav reviews progress of Great Indian Bustard Conservation, Grassland Restoration and Project Cheetah at Bhuj; Releases Gujarat Action Plan for GIB Conservation
Conservation succeeds when we Restore Whole Landscapes, Not Isolated Species: Union Environment Minister
Posted On: 13 SEP 2026 8:51PM by PIB Delhi

Union Minister for Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Shri Bhupender Yadav, today chaired a Review Meeting of Flagship Programmes at Bhuj, Kachchh (Gujarat), covering the conservation status of the Great Indian Bustard, grassland restoration and Project Cheetah. The Review Meeting was also attended by Shri Arjun Modhwadia, Cabinet Minister for Forest and Environment, Climate Change and Science & Technology, Government of Gujarat. Senior officials of the Union Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, the Gujarat Forest Department, the Wildlife Institute of India and the National Tiger Conservation Authority were also present.

On the occasion, the Union Minister emphasised that conservation must move beyond individual species to the restoration of entire landscapes, combining scientific management, habitat restoration and community participation, and said India is working towards becoming a global benchmark in landscape-level conservation.

Shri Yadav highlighted renewed efforts to conserve the Critically Endangered Great Indian Bustard (GIB) in Gujarat, where, he noted, Kachchh supports an important but small and isolated population. Releasing the Gujarat Action Plan for GIB Conservation, prepared by the Wildlife Institute of India in collaboration with the Gujarat Forest Department, the Minister said it provides a science-based roadmap to establish a minimum viable population of over 30 birds and secure 200–500 sq. km. of safe, contiguous habitat. He added that the immediate focus is on the approximately 200 sq. km. Lala–Rawa landscape, with interventions including habitat restoration, grazing management, invasive species removal, predator management and mitigation of infrastructure-related threats.

Shri Yadav informed that significant on-ground action has already been undertaken to secure this population. He noted that in Naliya, around 11 sq. km. of grassland infested with the invasive Prosopis juliflora has been restored, and the enclosure secured with 30 km of predator-proof fencing covering 15 sq. km., alongside targeted management of nest predators. Shri Yadav further emphasised that GIB conservation is ultimately the conservation of Kachchh's open natural ecosystems, which, he said, also support the lesser florican, chinkara, desert cats, raptors, vultures and other specialised wildlife.

Referring to a pioneering ‘jump-start’ intervention, in which infertile eggs laid by wild GIB females were replaced with viable eggs from the conservation breeding programme, the Minister said the resulting chick from the second such attempt has survived beyond the critical first three months in the wild – a landmark result for the species' recovery in Gujarat. He further stated that a GIB Soft Release Centre has been developed near Naliya, which will house and acclimatise captive-bred birds from Rajasthan ahead of their eventual release, once appropriate protocols and habitat conditions are in place.

On Grassland Restoration, Shri Yadav underlined the ecological importance of grasslands, which, he said, cover nearly 24% of India's land area but remain among the country's most degraded and under-conserved ecosystems. He informed that a proposed five-year national assessment, in collaboration with the Wildlife Institute of India, ICFRE and the Forest Survey of India, with National CAMPA support, would provide a scientific basis for developing a national framework for grassland management, focusing on mapping, ecological assessment, restoration and improved management of Open Natural Ecosystems, including Gujarat's Banni Grassland.

Reviewing Project Cheetah, the Minister noted that India has established a growing population from 29 founder cheetahs, with the population now reaching 52 individuals, including 49 cubs born in India. He observed that the cub survival rate in Kuno, at around 68%, significantly demonstrates the potential for successful population establishment under appropriate ecological conditions. Shri Yadav further noted that the protected habitat for cheetahs has expanded to 3,428 sq. km. through the integrated management of Kuno National Park and Gandhi Sagar, and that Banni Grasslands in Gujarat and Nauradehi Wildlife Sanctuary in Madhya Pradesh have been identified as future release sites. The Minister said the programme is increasingly moving towards landscape-level management, ensuring adequate habitat, prey base and ecological connectivity for the long-term recovery of the species.

2309866.title: Union Environment Minister presides over Workshop on Mangrove Conservation in Bhuj; Releases Key Mangrove Publications and Reviews MISHTI Progress
2309866.ministry: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
2309866.body_html:
Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
Union Environment Minister presides over Workshop on Mangrove Conservation in Bhuj; Releases Key Mangrove Publications and Reviews MISHTI Progress
Shri Bhupender Yadav stresses Scientific, Site-Specific and Community-Led Mangrove Restoration; Launches Mangrove GIS (MGIS) Portal for Decision Support
Posted On: 13 SEP 2026 8:00PM by PIB Delhi

Union Minister for Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Shri Bhupender Yadav, today addressed the Workshop on Mangrove Conservation, Restoration and Sustainable Management held at Bhuj, Kachchh (Gujarat). Addressing the workshop, the Minister emphasised that mangroves must be conserved as living ecosystems, given their importance for coastal biodiversity, fisheries, shoreline protection, climate resilience and livelihoods.

The workshop was also attended by and addressed by Shri Arjun Modhwadia, Cabinet Minister for Forest and Environment, Climate Change and Science & Technology, Government of Gujarat, and Shri Trikambhai Chhanga, Minister of State for Higher and Technical Education, Government of Gujarat, who reaffirmed the State Government's commitment to mangrove conservation and coastal ecosystem restoration under MISHTI.

Reviewing Gujarat's mangrove conservation efforts under the MISHTI (Mangrove Initiative for Shoreline Habitats & Tangible Incomes) programme, the Shri Yadav noted the emphasis on restoration, scientific management, community participation and technology-enabled monitoring. He informed that under MISHTI, Gujarat has made significant progress in mangrove restoration, with 27,652 hectares covered against the 2023–27 target of 29,250 hectares, including 12,450 hectares in the ecologically challenging Kori Creek region. He added that site-specific restoration techniques suited to the conditions of Kachchh have been adopted, alongside measures for biodiversity enhancement, seaweed cultivation and sustainable livelihoods.

On the occasion, the Minister released the Coffee Table Book on Kachchh Mangroves and the Mangroves Atlas of Gujarat, and launched the Mangrove GIS (MGIS) Portal, stating that these would strengthen science-based decision-making and monitoring of mangrove habitats across the state. Shri Yadav also felicitated the Guneri Inland Mangrove Village Biodiversity Management Committee, commending its sustained community-led conservation of the Guneri inland mangroves – a rare ecosystem thriving away from the coast – which, he noted, was declared Gujarat's first Biodiversity Heritage Site in January 2025.

The workshop was attended by senior officials of the Union Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change and the Gujarat Forest Department, along with scientists, conservationists and representatives of local communities engaged in mangrove restoration and coastal livelihood initiatives in Kachchh.

2309852.title: Union Home Minister and Minister of Cooperation Shri Amit Shah today addresses 52nd India Gems and Jewellery Awards ceremony in Mumbai as the Chief Guest
2309852.body_html:
Ministry of Home Affairs
Union Home Minister and Minister of Cooperation Shri Amit Shah today addresses 52nd India Gems and Jewellery Awards ceremony in Mumbai as the Chief Guest
India will emerge as the global hub for gems and jewellery in the coming years
The award recipients include exporters, manufacturers, bankers and women entrepreneurs; together, they have set new benchmarks for India’s growth
Era of lab-grown diamonds is now set to emerge, with the market expected to grow to nearly 50 times the size of the current diamond market
We must prepare ourselves in such a way that the entire ecosystem and the complete manufacturing value chain for lab-grown diamonds are in the hands of Indians
India should emerge as a pioneering industry in the new era of lab-grown diamonds, and the Modi Government is ready to provide all possible support to achieve this
Nine out of every ten diamonds cut and polished across the world are processed in Surat, city’s traders have not merely cut and polished diamonds; by generating employment for millions, they have also made a significant contribution to the economy and India’s exports
Mumbai, economic capital of the country, has made a significant contribution to establishing the gems and jewellery trade as a key pillar of India’s exports
The resolve of Prime Minister Modi to make India the world’s foremost nation in every sphere by 15 August 2047 has also been embraced by the 1.4 billion people of the country
Whenever India has faced a crisis, jewellery traders have always stood wholeheartedly with society and the nation
The foundation laid for these awards in 1975 has, over the past 50 years, evolved into a prestigious platform for India’s gems and jewellery industry, I congratulate everyone associated with the industry for its continuity, excellence and contribution to providing employment to millions of people
Posted On: 13 SEP 2026 7:46PM by PIB Delhi

Union Home Minister and Minister of Cooperation Shri Amit Shah today addressed the 52nd India Gems and Jewellery Awards ceremony in Mumbai as the Chief Guest. Maharashtra Chief Minister Shri Devendra Fadnavis, Deputy Chief Minister Shri Eknath Shinde, Gujarat Deputy Chief Minister Shri Harsh Sanghavi, and several other dignitaries were present on the occasion.

Addressing the awards ceremony, Union Home Minister and Minister of Cooperation Shri Amit Shah said that it is a matter of great happiness for him that the Gems and Jewellery Awards, which have continuously contributed to enhancing India’s economy, prosperity and global brilliance, are being conferred on so many distinguished achievers today. He said that this initiative of the India Diamond Board is a reflection of India’s confidence, skill, prosperity and global aspirations. India will emerge as the global hub for gems and jewellery in the coming years.

Union Home Minister and Minister of Cooperation Shri Amit Shah said that when the foundation of these awards was laid in 1975, hardly anyone could have imagined that this small initiative would, five decades later, evolve into a prestigious platform for the country’s gems and jewellery industry, and that the industry would play such a significant role in the growth of the national economy and the expansion of the MSME sector. Shri Shah said that those honoured today include exporters, manufacturers, bankers and women entrepreneurs. Together, they have set new benchmarks for India’s growth.

Shri Amit Shah said that gems and jewellery have always been an integral part of India’s identity. For over 6,000 years, gems and jewellery from India have been traded across the world. The Roman writer Pliny had written that Rome’s treasury was being depleted by its trade in Indian gems and spices, as the wealth earned by Rome was flowing to India through this trade. Shri Shah said that over the centuries, Indian artisans and craftsmen have continually added new dimensions to this tradition. During the medieval period, jewellery craftsmanship received royal patronage and reached new heights. The princely states of Rajasthan and Kolkata gave rise to the distinctive traditions of Kundan and Meenakari. Even today, Jaipur is renowned across the world as the capital of coloured gemstones. He said that any discussion on India’s gems and jewellery industry would remain incomplete without mentioning Surat. Shri Shah said that it is a fact that Surat has played a tremendous role in transforming the face of an entire industry. Nearly nine out of every ten diamonds cut and polished in the world are processed in Surat. He said that the people of Surat have not merely cut and polished diamonds; they have also demonstrated the highest standards of hard work and perseverance. The diamond merchants of Surat have not only provided employment to millions of people, enabled them to become self-reliant and made a significant contribution to the country’s economy and exports, but have also accomplished something even greater. He said that there was a time when it was believed that Kutch and Saurashtra would turn into a desert within fifty years. However, through their determination and relentless efforts to secure water for Kutch and Saurashtra, the diamond merchants of Surat also played a crucial role in saving the entire Saurashtra region.

Union Home Minister and Minister of Cooperation Shri Amit Shah said that Mumbai, the country’s financial capital, has made a significant contribution to establishing the gems and jewellery industry as a key pillar of India’s exports. The Bharat Diamond Bourse (BDB) has today emerged as a symbol of India’s gems and jewellery trade across the world.

Union Home Minister and Minister of Cooperation, Shri Amit Shah, said that the Government led by Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi has brought about several transformational changes in the country over the past 12 years. He said that in 2014, India was counted among the ‘Fragile Five’; today, it is among the top five economies of the world. He said that the GDP figures for the first quarter of the current financial year were released recently, and with a growth rate of 7.8 per cent, India has emerged as one of the fastest-growing major economies in the world. He said that this transformation has not been limited to economic activity alone; Prime Minister Modi has worked to bring about change across every sector. He said, “Who could have imagined that a terrorist attack would be answered by entering Pakistan’s territory, and that the country would have a Prime Minister capable of taking such a decisive stand?” Whether it was the surgical strike, the air strike or Operation Sindoor, Modi Ji has pursued a defence policy that makes the enemy think twice and tremble at the very thought of attacking India. He said that whether it is the construction of the Ram Janmabhoomi temple, the Kashi Vishwanath Corridor, the rejuvenation of Kedarnath or Mahakal Lok, India has accomplished what, for decades, people did not even have the courage to speak about.

Shri Amit Shah said that the transformational changes brought about by Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi in the field of infrastructure have given a major boost to the economy. Driven by PLI schemes and facilities aimed at promoting exports, India’s exports are continuing to surpass their own records. He said that Prime Minister Modi has given the 140 crore people of the country the confidence and resolve that by 15 August 2047, India will emerge as number one nation in the world across every sector. The people of India have also embraced this resolve. Shri Shah said that wherever global circumstances have changed and trade and commerce have required support, necessary initiatives have been undertaken. The Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Act, 2026 is the latest example of this. Companies engaged in the trading of rough diamonds in specially notified areas have been granted exemption from income tax for a period of 15 years. This marks a major beginning towards establishing India as the world’s rough diamond trading hub.

Union Home Minister and Minister of Cooperation Shri Amit Shah said that Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi recently inaugurated the Bharat Ratnam Mega Common Facility Centre at SEEPZ, Mumbai, as part of the transformational initiatives in the infrastructure sector. Spread across 1.25 lakh square feet, the centre is equipped with state-of-the-art facilities such as 3D printing, casting and refining. He said that the India Jewellery Park is a landmark project that is expected to attract an investment of around ₹50,000 crore and generate direct and indirect employment for one lakh people. The Maharashtra Government has also extended several incentives, including exemption from stamp duty, concessions on electricity and enhanced subsidy rates. He said that in 2025, the industry had reached ₹2.44 lakh crore, accounting for 6.3 per cent of the country’s merchandise exports. The industry is providing direct and indirect employment to around 75 lakh people.

Shri Amit Shah said that India has today emerged as a major source of jewellery imports for the United States, the Middle East, Hong Kong and Europe, and that this journey must be taken forward. He said that the Free Trade Agreements entered into by the Government of India’s Ministry of Commerce with the European Union, the United Arab Emirates, Australia, Oman and the United Kingdom can serve as a major avenue for expanding our trade. He said that with the support of the Government of India, we must move forward with confidence and determination to explore new markets, new avenues of trade and new opportunities. Today, India processes more than 90 per cent of the world’s cut and polished diamonds, which is the strongest testament to the courage and enterprise of India’s jewellery industry.

Union Home Minister and Minister of Cooperation Shri Amit Shah said that times are changing and so are consumer trends, and this transformation presents a significant opportunity for the gems and jewellery trade. He said that jewellers should be prepared to seize the opportunities arising from these changes. He said that the era of lab-grown diamonds is now set to emerge, with the market expected to grow to nearly 50 times the size of the current diamond market. This represents a tremendous opportunity. He said that when the global jewellery trade underwent modernization, India was under colonial rule. Several countries moved ahead of us, including even smaller nations. But with the advent of the lab-grown diamond era, India has the necessary infrastructure, skills, capital and capable entrepreneurs. He said that we must prepare ourselves in such a way that the entire ecosystem and the complete manufacturing value chain for lab-grown diamonds are in the hands of Indians. Whether it is manufacturing the machines, producing lab-grown diamonds, making jewellery, or developing Indian brands and opening showrooms in cities across the world, the entire value chain should be within our reach. He said that Indian jewellery traders are fully capable of achieving this. Shri Shah said that the Government of India has already taken the initiative, while some enterprising traders in Surat and Mumbai have also taken the lead. The Governments of Gujarat and Maharashtra are bringing in supportive policies, and the Government of India will also introduce appropriate policies. He said that from manufacturing the machines to the showroom where the jewellery ultimately reaches a woman’s hand, India must have ownership of the entire ecosystem, and the industry must move forward with this vision and ambition. He said that merely increasing the pace of work will no longer be sufficient; the scale of operations must also be transformed. Shri Shah said that India should emerge as a pioneering industry in the new era of lab-grown diamonds, and Indian brands should become global brands, ensuring a strong presence for India and Indian jewellery traders in this global business. For this, the Modi Government is ready to provide all possible support.

Union Home Minister and Minister of Cooperation Shri Amit Shah said that whenever Gujarat or India has faced a crisis, the jewellery industry has always stood wholeheartedly with society and the nation. The gems and jewellery industry has never shied away from contributing to the advancement and welfare of society. Whether it was a drought, a flood, a cyclone, water conservation, tree plantation, or ensuring that the children of artisans and employees receive education at the finest institutions, the industry has consistently contributed to the progress of society. For this, I wholeheartedly commend and congratulate the industry. He expressed hope that the leading industrial houses, young entrepreneurs and technologists present here would leave with the resolve that, in the diamond world of the future, the entire value chain should be built in India, and that the marketing chain across the world should also be led by Indian brands.
